title: ME08B: How Real Change Travels
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Richard Claydon continues his Leadership, Rewritten series with a narrative about Maya, a leader whose well-planned change initiative stalled because she moved too far ahead of her stakeholders. He argues that change spreads through networks, learning and trust rather than hierarchy, and he frames three team rituals (Cooperation, Curiosity and Connection) as the connective tissue of organisational flexibility, using a gym analogy throughout. The Cooperation ritual maps the quarter of stakeholders whose early backing can carry an idea and translates the pitch into each group's own dialect. The Curiosity ritual rotates formats such as a failure fair and a future backcast so that learning is harvested rather than merely discussed. The Connection ritual pairs people across functions for short conversations about what energises and drains them. Claydon warns that rituals decay into theatre when form replaces purpose, and closes with three micro-exercises leaders can try this month.
points: Change fails less from bad ideas than from thin networks, so legitimacy has to be built before launch by securing the roughly 25 percent of stakeholders who can carry an idea through resistance.
Persuasion works by translating one initiative into the language each function cares about, which turns selling change into distributing ownership.
Curiosity rituals must vary each quarter and end with a harvested artefact, so that learning accumulates instead of staying episodic.
Cross-silo conversations about energy and drain thicken relational tissue, and bottlenecks clear faster even though nothing formal changes.
Rituals collapse into theatre when people perform the posture without the intent, and a ritual that drains energy should be stopped and its purpose reset.
quotes: Most change dies not from bad ideas but from thin networks. Brilliant solutions wither because legitimacy isn’t built.

The shift was subtle but profound: they weren’t “selling change,” they were distributing ownership. And when Finance questioned a detail mid-way, Priya didn’t defend—she reconvened, explained, and re-secured the agreement.
Each ritual closed with a harvest—a small artefact that travelled forward: a checklist, a provocation, a rule to break. Learning became cumulative rather than episodic.
Weeks later, bottlenecks cleared faster, emails softened, and help arrived unasked. Nothing formal had changed, yet everything moved easier.
The pattern was consistent: rituals failed when form replaced purpose. When people performed the posture but not the intent.
Before your next initiative, map the 25 percent who can carry it. If you can’t name them, you’re not ready to move.
